stories.headline: U.S. pushes allies, China to back Trump’s economic war on Iran
stories.deck: U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s comments underscored how Mr. Trump is shifting to economic rather than military pressure on Tehran the war drags toward the six-month mark
stories.bodyText:
The United States on Thursday (August 20, 2026) warned allies and China to join President Donald Trump’s new campaign to isolate the Iranian economy, vowing that Washington would “collapse this regime” in Tehran.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s comments underscored how Mr. Trump is shifting to economic rather than military pressure on Tehran as the war drags toward the six-month mark.
Iran branded the U.S. threats as “economic terrorism” and said they would fail.
Under fire at home over the impact of the war and with crucial midterm elections looming, Trump had on Wednesday (August 19, 2026) promised the “most crushing” economic operation ever against Iran.
“It is going to work in Iran and we are going to collapse this regime,” Mr. Bessent told U.S. broadcaster CNBC.
Neither Mr. Trump nor his treasury chief has set out the measures they are planning against Iran. Bessent said he would give more details during a press conference on Monday (August 24, 2026).
But Mr. Bessent underlined that Washington expects both allies and rivals to join in.
“This is going to be the greatest coordinated economic isolation in the history of the world. And we are going to them and saying you are either with us or against us,” he added in a message to allies.
Asked whether the United States would pressure China, Mr. Bessent said that “many conversations are best to have in private” but called on Beijing “to get with the program.”
Chinese President Xi Jinping is due to visit the White House on September 24.
‘Crimes against humanity’
Mr. Bessent’s comments marked a notable return by a senior U.S. official to talking about regime change in Iran, after months of Trump insisting that the goal of the war is to stop Tehran from getting a nuclear weapon.
But the U.S. treasury boss said the economic plan meant the United States is less likely to have to return to heavy military operations against Iran.
“If we are doing the maximum economic pressure, then that means that likely there will not be a large-scale kinetic restart, but I will emphasise that is for now,” Mr. Bessent said.
Iran dismissed Trump’s plan
“The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America’s own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on X.
The Iranian Foreign Ministry blasted the U.S. threats, which come after years of damaging American sanctions against Tehran.
“Undoubtedly, the U.S. economic sanctions against Iran, which have targeted the fundamental human rights of every Iranian citizen, are a case of ‘economic terrorism’ and ‘crimes against humanity’,” it said in a statement carried by state media.
Despite the heavy international sanctions, Iran found ways to continue exporting its oil, with China the biggest buyer. Tehran operates a so-called shadow fleet of tankers, all of which are under international sanctions.

stories.headline: Noel Tata kicks off hunt for next Tata Sons chief
stories.deck: Trusts Chairman Noel Tata, Another Trustee Meet HDFC's Ex-Chairman Deepak Parekh
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata is understood to have informally kicked off the search process for Tata Sons' eighth chairman, meeting former HDFC chairman 
Deepak Parekh
 at the Taj Wellington Mews Residences in Mumbai on Wednesday, according to people aware of the meeting.
The meeting, which also included another Trusts trustee and was held after Tuesday's adjourned Tata Sons annual general meeting, is understood to have focused on the proposed succession committee that will oversee the selection of the next chairman of the $185 billion Tata Group's holding company.
The committee is required under Tata Sons' Articles of Association and will lead the search for a successor to N Chandrasekaran, who has decided to step down when his current chairmanship term ends in February 2027.
Trusts chairman Noel Tata, another trustee meet HDFC’s ex-chairman Deepak Parekh
It could not be established whether Parekh was offered a role on the succession panel. Noel Tata's office did not respond to a request for comment, while Parekh could not be reached for comment.
Parekh is no stranger to the Tata Group. During his years leading HDFC, the financial services group maintained significant business ties with the Tata conglomerate. He also served on the board of Indian Hotels Company, the Tata Group's flagship hospitality company. 
During the boardroom battle that followed Cyrus Mistry's removal as Tata Sons chairman in 2016, Parekh was among those who publicly backed Mistry. Under Tata Sons' Articles, the succession committee must comprise five members, three nominated by Sir Dorabji Tata Trust (SDTT) and Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), and two selected by the Tata Sons board.
One of the board representatives is expected to be an existing Tata Sons director, such as independent directors Harish Manwani or Anita George, while the other can be an external independent member.
The three trust nominees need not necessarily be SDTT's and SRTT's representatives on the Tata Sons board, according to the articles. The committee's formation faces a hurdle, though. The Articles require the three trust nominees to be "jointly nominated by SDTT and SRTT", meaning they cannot be appointed by SDTT alone. With SRTT under a regulatory restriction, it remains unclear how the formal process will move forward.
The search committee model has been used before at Tata Sons. Cyrus Mistry was selected in 2012 through a similar process to succeed Ratan Tata. Following Mistry's removal in 2016, a five-member committee comprising Ratan Tata, Trusts trustee Venu Srinivasan, former Trusts trustee Amit Chandra, ex-Tata Sons director Ronen Sen and Prof Kumar Bhattacharyya was tasked with identifying a successor, eventually selecting Chandrasekaran.
The succession exercise also comes against the backdrop of a long-standing governance question at the Tata Group: the balance of power between Tata Sons' executive leadership and Trusts, its controlling shareholder. The issue came to the fore during Mistry's ouster in 2016 and has resurfaced with Chandrasekaran's decision to step down in 2027.

stories.headline: Ex-Pak PM Imran Khan moved to private hospital from prison after SC order
stories.bodyText:
Imprisoned former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan was shifted from Adiala prison to a private hospital in Islamabad after midnight Thursday for a medical examination, news agency AP reported citing Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party's statement.
Khan was taken to Shifa International Hospital hours after Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry said the government would comply with a Supreme Court order directing authorities to facilitate his medical examination.
The PTI said the transfer was carried out following the Supreme Court's order earlier this week but did not provide further details. It remained unclear whether Khan would return to prison after the examination or stay at the hospital for further treatment. His family and party have sought permission for him to remain there.
Earlier Thursday, Chaudhry said the government had approached the Supreme Court seeking clarification on whether the medical relief granted to Khan applied only to him or could also cover other prisoners. He stressed that the request was not aimed at delaying or defying the court's order.
The three-judge Supreme Court panel had ordered authorities two days earlier to take Khan to Shifa International Hospital for a medical examination amid prolonged concerns raised by his family and personal doctors over his health and access to treatment. 
The court directed that a medical board examine him, including specialists and his personal physician, Faisal Sultan.
The government has maintained that prisoners receive medical care under existing rules and can be moved to government hospitals when required.
Concerns over Khan's health intensified in January after his family claimed he had lost about 85% of the vision in his right eye. The government disputed the claim and later said his vision had improved by around 70%.
Khan, a former cricket star, was ousted as prime minister in a parliamentary no-confidence vote in April 2022. He has remained imprisoned since 2023 after convictions in multiple cases, including a graft case.

stories.headline: Bengaluru hugs its oldest rock to save it from a tunnel
stories.deck: At Lalbagh, Bengaluru citizens are embracing a 3.3-billion-year-old rock — and threatening a 10,000-strong march — to stop the Hebbal–Silk Board Tunnel Road from passing beneath the park
stories.bodyText:
Jyotsna Basotia
On Sunday mornings at Lalbagh, a small but growing crowd has gathered for the past three weeks. Children, retirees and walkers form a human chain, walk up to a rock and put their arms around it. The rock is Peninsular Gneiss, a geological formation inside Bengaluru’s oldest botanical garden that dates back more than 3.3 billion years. It has become the centrepiece of a campaign against the proposed Hebbal–Silk Board Tunnel Road, a roughly 17-km underground corridor intended to cut travel time between the city’s north and south.
What happened
S Umesh Kumar, President of Lalbagh and Cubbon Park Walkers’ Association, says, “More than a hundred people joined demonstrations on August 2 and August 9. We are now planning a larger protest at Freedom Park, with up to 10,000 people, including students, environmentalists and celebrities like Sanjana Naidu and Sonika Gowda.”
B V Sridhar Rao, who has walked in Lalbagh for over 30 years, is quick to point out that this isn’t the first time walkers have organised to protect Lalbagh. An earlier Metro proposal would have demolished part of the garden wall and felled nearly 400 trees, while a proposed multi-level parking complex would have taken up about five acres. 
Both plans were pushed back. “Every time, we’ve had to fight to keep the garden as it is,” says Sridhar, “Now it’s the rock.”
Why the rock at Lalbagh matters
“I was a boy when I started walking,” Sridhar fondly remembers, “I am not the first generation to walk at Lalbagh. My grandfather walked here, then my father, then myself, and now my daughter — that’s four generations.” Umesh, who lives less than a kilometre from the garden, puts it more simply: “We grew up playing here, in Lalbagh and in Cubbon Park.” “So many people come to Lalbagh to walk, run and jog for their physical health,” Suma B V, Organising Secretary at Lalbagh and Cubbon Park Walkers’ Association says, “It’s not that Bengaluru has no other parks. But this is the oldest one we have, going back to our earliest years. We’re asking the government to please set this project aside and think of another way.”
What protesters fear: A cracked rock and a vanished lake
Walkers are particularly worried about vibrations from tunnelling or rock-cutting travelling through the ground near Lalbagh Lake. “The lake bed is a mud base, not concrete,” Sridhar says, adding, “Even a small capillary formed in the soil will be enough. Water will find its own way. As the water starts flowing, it can eventually become a big orifice in the underground. The lake will lose its water holding capacity.” Umesh adds, “If you go a hundred or two hundred feet under a rock formation like this, the whole thing gets damaged. Once that happens, you can’t undo it. Putting in steel supports afterward is no use. That’s just artificial.” A soil test conducted at the site has also angered the protesters. Sridhar argues, “When an appeal is pending, they should wait for the court’s direction before sending samples to the laboratory.”
The bigger question: Does Bengaluru need this tunnel?
The walkers insist they are not opposed to the tunnel project itself. “We are not against development,” Umesh says. “We are against the tunnel going under Lalbagh. That rock is our heritage. The route can be changed. Why does it have to pass under Lalbagh and Cubbon Park? These are the two eyes of Bengaluru.” Suma echoes the point. “We’ve been protesting for three weeks now to save the rock — it sits on six to eight acres, and the tunnel is meant to pass right beneath it,” she says, adding, “We are not against the project. We are against it passing through Lalbagh. The road runs all the way from Hebbal to Silk Board — there must be a way to build it that doesn’t cross the garden.” She also connects the fight to the city’s air quality. “COVID taught us how much we depend on clean air,” she says. “Where do we get that, if not from our parks? The city is already polluted enough.”
What happens next in court
PIL petitions filed against the project, scheduled before the High Court for August 20, have now been adjourned to September 3. The walkers’ association is urging the government to reconsider the project. Umesh says, “Before the next hearing, we will discuss with all members how to take the initiative forward. We believe the court will give the right judgment.” Sridhar too remains hopeful the court will rule in the protesters’ favour once the scientific and technical arguments are heard.

stories.headline: Dating beyond the apps: Where are Bengaluru’s singles meeting now?
stories.bodyText:
Tired of finding love through a screen? Perhaps the next match is waiting somewhere beyond the app. For years, dating in Bengaluru has been just a swipe away. Open an app, set your preferences, scroll through profiles and wait for a match. But as dating apps become a familiar part of urban relationships, some singles are asking a different question: What if you simply met someone in real life?
Conducted in August 2024, a 
Rakuten Insight
 survey of 21,812 Indian respondents aged 16 and above — 9,239 women and 12,573 men — found that a large majority did not use mobile dating apps. The findings suggest that for a sizeable section of Indians, meeting someone offline remains the norm rather than a return to it.
Swipe fatigue is real, but the desire to date hasn’t disappeared. A June 2026 
Economic Times report, which spoke to two dozen Indian singles aged 25 to 35, found several describing exhaustion with the “dating hamster wheel”. Some were turning to singles mixers and personalised matchmaking services, signalling a desire for something that feels less transactional and more personal.
In Bengaluru, that search is taking people to places that have little to do with dating — running tracks, book clubs, workshops, concerts, treks, cafés and even introductions arranged by friends.
Friends are the new algorithms
Before dating apps turned compatibility into a set of filters, there was always the friend who knew someone who would be “perfect for you”. That old-fashioned system is finding new takers among singles who would rather have some context before meeting a potential partner.
‘My friends know me better than an algorithm’ is becoming common among those who are tired of making decisions based on a few photographs and carefully curated answers. And there is another advantage — even if the introduction doesn’t lead to romance, there is often a shared social circle to fall back on.
From hobbies to chemistry
Perhaps the most organic route to romance is one where dating isn’t the primary objective at all. Running and cycling groups, trekking communities, book clubs, dance classes, pottery workshops, board-game groups and other interest-based communities are giving singles an opportunity to meet people while doing something they genuinely enjoy.
Arpita Nag, a 29-year-old working professional, says it’s easier to meet people who share similar hobbies. “I like meeting people through activities because you get to see who they really are. You’re not judging someone based on just bios, pictures and pick-up lines; you’re talking, laughing and spending time together, and sometimes that naturally turns into something more.”
The return of the singles event
Speed dating may sound like something from another era, but singles mixers, curated meet-ups, brunches and other dating events are making a comeback. For people who want to meet someone offline but don’t have an extensive social circle, such events offer a middle ground.
Saurav Arya, founder of Small World, which organises speed dating events across the country, says Bengaluru has become a natural hub for offline dating because so many young professionals live independently and are looking to build new social circles. “When your entire week is consumed by work, you don’t want to spend your weekend swiping. People want to meet, talk and see if there’s a connection. There’s a growing appetite for spaces where people can connect without the pressure of finding ‘the one’. That is what makes offline dating events work,” he shares.
The third-place romance
Then there are the places where nobody goes specifically to date. A café where the same people turn up every weekend. A bookstore hosting a discussion. A concert where strangers bond over a favourite musician. A comedy show where two people end up laughing at the same jokes. A cultural event where a conversation continues after the programme ends.
These “third places” — social spaces outside home and work — can provide something dating apps struggle to replicate: repeated, unplanned encounters.
Bengaluru’s new dating playbook Friends: Personal introductions and setups
Running/cycling groups: Regular company without dating pressure 
Book clubs: Shared interests that spark conversation 
Dance/pottery/workshops:
 Bonding while learning something new 
Trekking groups:
 Miles, memories, and shared adventures 
Board-game communities: Relaxed settings for easy interaction 
Singles mixers: Spaces where everyone is open to meet someone 
Concerts & cultural events: Common interests that create natural openings 
Cafés & bookstores: Bengaluru’s ‘third places’ for casual encounters
Professional networks: Connections through work and industry circles

Key takeaway:
 Dating-app use is far from universal 
Why some quit:
 Boredom was among the leading reasons
Source: Rakuten Insight, August 2024; data reported by Statista.

stories.headline: Karnataka SIR: Over 43.80 lakh voters to get notice; over 20 lakh flagged for ‘logical discrepancy’
stories.deck: Notices will be served to 23.45 lakh people who could not find their own or their parents’ details in the 2002 electoral roll
stories.bodyText:
The Office of the Chief Electoral Officer, Karnataka, has identified more than 20.35 lakh voters whose enumeration forms contain “logical discrepancies”. These discrepancies or anomalies have been identified under nine categories.
Besides this, notices will be served to another 23.45 lakh people who could not find their own or their parents’ details in the 2002 electoral roll.
Together, 43.80 lakh notices will be served across Karnataka, of which 24.05 lakh are concentrated in Bengaluru alone.
Apart from Bengaluru, the districts reporting a high number of logical discrepancies include Mandya, Kolar, Dakshina Kannada and Chikkamagaluru. Mandya recorded 1.30 lakh discrepancies, more than the 1.12 lakh reported in BBMP South.
The categories of anomalies include an implausible gap between a parent/grandparent and progeny, a parent who is also present in the current enrolment of an SIR State is considered invalid, resulting in anomalies for all progenies mapped to that parent’s last SIR record; and different father’s names in case of both progeny and self mapping.
In cases where a different name or father’s name is mentioned, “different” can also refer to a spelling variation between documents. For instance, if a person’s father’s name is misspelt and the spelling differs from that in the father’s own document, it too can be flagged as a logical discrepancy.
Another peculiar category relates to progeny mapping. If a voter has linked themselves to a parent or relative who appears in the current enrolment of an SIR State but is later found invalid and excluded from the final electoral roll, all progenies mapped to that person’s last SIR record will also be flagged as anomalies. In other words, officials in the CEO’s office said that if a parent’s case is deemed suspect and the parent does not make it to the final roll, the same issue will extend to the progenies linked to them.

stories.headline: GBA’s Freedom from Waste campaign: Will it be enough to keep Bengaluru’s 1,616 blackspots from reappearing?
stories.deck: Each blackspot represents the larger interaction between collection efficiency, waste processing capacity, enforcement, and institutional coordination. Thus, clearing these blackspots may remove the symptom, only for it to reappear within a short time.
stories.bodyText:
On 1 August, 2026, the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) launched a month-long ‘Freedom from Waste’ campaign, marking the first city-wide cleanliness initiative since the Bruhat Bengaluru Mahanagara Palike (BBMP) transitioned to GBA.
Several agencies, including the city’s five corporations, Bengaluru Solid Waste Management Limited (BSWML), Rail Infrastructure Development Company (Karnataka) Limited, and Bengaluru Metro Rail Corporation Limited, are working in close collaboration to target 1,616 locations or blackspots holding approximately 22,732 tonnes of waste.
As part of this, authorities had directed property owners to clear waste from their vacant plots by 15 August, failing which civic agencies would undertake the cleaning and recover the cost through property tax. While clearing waste is an essential first step, it is important to understand why these blackspots emerge in the first place.
A symptom, not the cause
A holistic approach through a systems lens highlights that blackspots are not the cause of Bengaluru’s waste crisis but just a symptom of a fundamental problem. Each blackspot represents the larger interaction between collection efficiency, waste processing capacity, enforcement, and institutional coordination. Thus, clearing these blackspots may remove the symptom, only for it to reappear within a short time.
One of the key drivers of these blackspots is the inconsistent waste collection. On paper, Bengaluru has a city-wide door-to-door waste collection system; however, the auto-tipper model — the backbone of the daily collection system — is highly stressed.
According to the BSWML, one auto-tipper is expected to service around 750 households, making collection impractical and resulting in irregular waste collection. Although there have been past efforts to improve waste collection and the campaign also acknowledges this as one of the focus areas, the implementation roadmap for strengthening door-to-door collection models is not clearly outlined.
Further, a city that experiences intermittent waste collection with no bins around pushes the public to dump waste in open areas. Vacant plots and street corners are often perceived as convenient dumping locations, especially for wet waste, which is difficult to manage and store at homes, as it produces foul odours and attracts flies. As these waste piles grow, it encourages people to dump waste at the same location, increasing the burden for municipalities to clear the blackspot.
Shifting the burden of waste
Another systemic challenge is the tendency to shift the burden of waste, with collected waste often ending up in landfills located on the city’s outskirts. Under this campaign, GBA has identified 8 land parcels, covering nearly 57 acres on the outskirts, where the collected waste will be transported.
While sites such as Kannur and Chikkajala have existing construction and demolition (C&D) waste processing plants, there is limited public information on the processing facilities for the remaining sites, which account for nearly 75% of the identified land. Thus, transporting waste may provide an immediate solution for the blackspots, but it raises a broader systems question of whether these sites act as temporary aggregation points or merely shift the waste to the outskirts, which slowly become permanent waste relocation sites.
Further, Bengaluru has witnessed such cases in places such as Mavallipura and Mandur, where peripheral dumping evolved into long-term environmental and health challenges for people living in these locations.
Effective coordination
With the city continuously expanding, large-scale infrastructure projects such as metro construction generate a substantial amount of C&D waste. This C&D material forms the foundation of many blackspots in the city, over which municipal solid waste (MSW) accumulates, making them a permanent dumping spot. Also, C&D waste consists of high-value material that can be recovered and recycled, but when this gets mixed with MSW, it loses its economic value.
While the Environment (Construction and Demolition) Waste Management Rules, 2025, highlight the specific management needs and provisions for proper clearance, effective coordination between generators, transporters, collection agencies, and recyclers is crucial to avoid disrupting end-to-end operations.
To sum up, several reforms over the years have shaped the waste situation in Bengaluru. Each addressed a specific bottleneck and took action to curb it. Yet, there is a need to look beyond optimising individual components and understand the interdependencies within a system — those that weaken results and lead to recurring blackspots.
Viewed from a systems lens, the Freedom from Waste campaign offers an opportunity, as it brings together multiple civic agencies under a common objective. If coordinated efforts extend beyond clearing blackspots, it could address the drivers beneath illegal dumping. The success of this initiative could help build public trust and encourage greater citizen participation, turning a cleanliness initiative into a long-term shift towards cleaner Bengaluru.
Anushree Aggrawal and Pooja Verma work as analysts in the Sustainability group at the Center for Study of Science, Technology and Policy (CSTEP), a research-based think tank.

briefs.headline: Gangs of Bandipur: Do imported guns in Karnataka farmhouse hint at wildlife poaching?
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The Aug 15 Hanur encounter in which three hunters were killed has blown the lid off a larger malaise lurking in the woods at the trijunction of Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, and Kerala: sudden and shocking proliferation of modern, imported and automatic firearms, whose firepower is definitely more deadly than that of forest personnel.
The forests of Bandipur — a safe and popular weekend escape for Bengaluru’s young crowd — have become a hunting ground, with miscreants possessing guns imported from or manufactured in the US, Germany, Switzerland and Taiwan, besides several rounds of live ammunition. These include sub-machine guns — a strong suggestion that poachers may have access to a far more sophisticated arsenal than previously known.
“Till now, we’ve seen cheap country-made guns being used by poachers. Recent raids on a farmhouse in Karnataka have pointed to the presence of these advanced weapons,” a senior forest department official said.
The latest seizure came during a raid on a farmhouse at Kebbepura village in the Kundakere Range of Bandipur Tiger Reserve on Aug 18. According to a wildlife offence case registered by forest officials before the civil judge and judicial magistrate at Gundlupet, Chamarajanagar district, the seized weapons included a Swiss-made SG552-2 Commando assault rifle, a German-made APX single-barrel rifle, a Taiwanese HFC airsoft submachine gun, an old revolver, a JPX Jet Protector, a US-made Marlin rifle and several rounds of live ammunition.
The discovery is particularly worrying because Bandipur is not an isolated forest patch. Its location along the Karnataka-Tamil Nadu-Kerala landscape makes it part of a vast and interconnected wildlife corridor. The focus of the department has shifted from individual poachers to the possibility of organised networks supplying firearms to hunters operating in protected forests.
Alarmed by the developments, forest minister Ramalinga Reddy has written to home minister Priyank Kharge, seeking a coordinated crackdown on illegal weapons entering Karnataka, particularly along stretches passing through protected areas.
“We were shocked to see sophisticated and advanced weapons along the protected forests. While a few of the weapons had licences, most were unlicensed and appeared to have been sourced through local supply channels. This raises serious concerns. We are chalking out plans in collaboration with officials of the Southern Range to crack down on large-scale presence of such weapons and seize all illegal firearms,” minister Reddy told 
TOI
.
Forest officials recovered 48 deer and sambar antlers, a deer skull with an antler, bones of wild animals and pelts from the farmhouse that belonged to Senetila Lang Kumer, who is at large. The weapons were registered in the name of his uncle Jacob, who is also absconding.
Officials said the farmhouse manager had claimed that the weapons were sports guns or meant for game hunting. But an officer countered: “Regardless of their stated purpose, these weapons can be used to kill animals at short and medium ranges because of their firepower. Compared to the weapons carried by forest personnel, such as slide-action guns, these are far more advanced. We do not know why these firearms were kept at the farmhouse. We have registered a case under the Wildlife Protection Act,” the officer said.
Activists have urged the forest department and Karnataka govt to invoke provisions of the Arms Act against those found in possession of illegal weapons. Conservation volunteers said many illegal country-made weapons are sourced through dealers and middlemen in North India.

briefs.headline: Over 2 lakh cab drivers linked to Bengaluru aggregators, but govt lacks data on locals
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 For the first time, the state govt has revealed the scale of Bengaluru’s app-based cab workforce, estimating that over two lakh drivers are currently associated with ride-hailing aggregators. However, the govt admitted it has no data on how many of these drivers are Bengaluru residents and how many have migrated from other states in search of a livelihood.
According to data, 
Ola
 has around 45,000 drivers, 
Uber
 77,000 and Rapido 75,000 on their platforms. Together, the three aggregators account for an estimated 1.97 lakh drivers. Overall, more than two lakh drivers are estimated to be associated with app-based cab aggregators in Bengaluru.
The city has a total of 2.97 lakh registered cabs, including those operated by independent travel agencies.
The disclosure comes amid growing complaints from local taxi drivers’ unions that aggregators are drawing drivers from other states by offering better pay, incentives and other benefits, leaving local drivers struggling to find employment.
Transport minister Byrathi Suresh said the govt had noticed that “people from other states were registering in large numbers as drivers with app-based aggregators”, leading to distress among local drivers amid limited employment opportunities.
The issue gained traction on social media last week, with videos circulating of youngsters from Kerala, Assam and some north Indian states driving cabs on Bengaluru roads. Several Kannada activists questioned the transport minister’s silence over the alleged loss of driving jobs for locals. They also pointed to neighbouring Maharashtra’s move to crack down on commercial vehicle drivers who do not have a “working knowledge” of Marathi.
The govt, however, pointed to the eligibility requirements under Rule 8 of the Karnataka On-Demand Transportation Technology Aggregators Rules, 2016. Under the rules, a taxi driver must have been a resident of Karnataka for at least two years and possess a working knowledge of Kannada and one other language, preferably English.
The issue also came up in the legislative council Thursday, with Congress member Vinay Karthik seeking to know whether drivers with criminal antecedents were operating vehicles attached to aggregators.
On passenger safety, the govt said Vehicle Location Tracking Devices and emergency panic buttons have been installed in public service vehicles under the Nirbhaya scheme. When a panic button is activated, an alert is sent to the control room, which immediately forwards the alert to the police control room.
The minister said aggregators are also required to ensure police verification of the antecedents of every taxi driver before allowing them to operate on their platforms.

briefs.headline: Old Airport Road footpaths leave Bengaluru’s pedestrians with nowhere to walk
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: Pedestrians on Old Airport Road between Marathahalli and Kundalahalli Gate are being forced to step onto the busy carriageway to get past a series of footpath obstructions. The problem is particularly acute near Kundalahalli Gate underpass, where a commercial complex has enclosed a section of the footpath within its compound, citing pending land compensation.
The road connecting Marathahalli, Kundalahalli Gate and Varthur Kodi is a key route towards Whitefield and carries heavy traffic through the day. While footpaths have improved at some locations, residents said the stretch near the underpass remains difficult to negotiate because of waterlogging, parked and moving two-wheelers, cables, Bescom equipment and a bus shelter.
Aparna Khatri, a Marathahalli resident, said the combination of these problems makes walking difficult. “Two-wheelers are parked and even driven on the pavement, while hanging and tangled cables and Bescom equipment further obstruct the footpath. There is also constant waterlogging towards Kundalahalli Gate signal, making a large part of the road unusable,” she said.
Another resident said poor pedestrian infrastructure is influencing how people travel. 
“Even for places within walking distance, we prefer to take a car because walking is so difficult, especially when it rains. I stay five minutes from my workplace, but take a car, which takes 20 minutes. This is also one reason there are so many cars on the roads,” the resident said.
Having lived in the area for 12 years, the resident said footpaths have improved near Whitefield and Kundalahalli signal, but this stretch has remained problematic. The resident also recalled an elderly man suffering a head injury after being hit by a bike while walking near the spot.
The resident said the ongoing ‘Safe Footpaths’ drive should also cover the area. “The medical student who died a few months ago near RR Medical College after a truck ran over her was my friend’s daughter. Even recently, there was a case of a woman dying after skidding off a bike. These incidents happen and the authorities do nothing.”
The stretch is part of Old Airport Road, where Bengaluru Smart Infrastructure Ltd (B-Smile) is undertaking works under the high-density corridor project. The 19.5km corridor runs from ASC Centre to Kadugodi via Varthur Kodi.
A B-Smile assistant executive engineer said he was trying to address the issue by writing to Bengaluru East City Corporation authorities. “We’re constantly facing hurdles from property owners and influential locals who interfere with ongoing works and create conflict,” he said.
On the commercial complex, he said the property owner has alleged that compensation has not been paid. “We can only take up works; the responsibility for clearing encroachments rests with corporation officials,” he said.

briefs.headline: Festival rush proves costly for Bengaluru woman as thieves steal her Rs 4 lakh chain
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru:
 Varamahalakshmi festival shopping turned into a nightmare for an Ayurvedic doctor after thieves targeted her in the crowded KR Market and made away with a 29-gram gold chain worth over Rs 4 lakh.
R Karuna Shree, a Basaveshwaranagar resident, left home around 12.30pm Tuesday to buy flowers, fruits, vegetables and other puja essentials. She reached KR Market around 1pm and later went to the ground floor of Sri Krishna Rajendra Market Complex at 1.45pm to buy jasmine flowers.
While shopping at a jasmine stall, she suddenly felt someone touch her neck from behind. Startled, she instinctively brought her hands forward and realised something was wrong.
“I held my gold chain tightly and turned around to find a few women. As I screamed for help, the women distanced themselves from me,” Karuna told 
TOI
.
She continued shopping and went upstairs to buy betel leaves. It was only when she checked her neck again that she realised her 29-gram gold chain was missing. She rushed home and, after discussing the incident with her sister, went to City Market police station and filed a complaint.
“I’ve been shopping alone in the market and the Chickpet area for the past 10 years, but this is the first time I’ve become a victim of crime. I preferred KR Market because jasmine flowers are usually not available in other small markets,” she said. The chain also held sentimental value for Karuna. “I bought it by taking tuitions for students after I stopped practising and was in a bad financial state,” she said.
A senior police officer said patrolling is challenging because of the crowds. “Thousands of people visit KR Market and Chickpet for shopping; it is difficult for police to even patrol,” the officer said.
A case has been registered under BNS Section 303 (theft), and police are trying to identify and nab the culprits.

briefs.headline: Landlord, 60, sexually harasses student at flat in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A 20-year-old undergraduate student has accused her 60-year-old apartment owner of sexually harassing her during a visit to her flat in Langford Town recently.
According to the complaint filed by 
Manya
 (name changed), the man forcibly hugged her, kissed on cheeks and touched her inappropriately despite her attempts to move away and resist his advances.
Manya has been living on the second floor of the apartment on Berlie Street for 2.5 months. The accused, Kamalesh Kumar visited her flat around 6.30pm on Aug 15 to inspect pending repair work.
Kumar enquired her about her college and then held her hand, pretending to examine the mehendi on it. When she attempted to pull her hand away, he allegedly pulled her towards him and hugged her. He then kissed her and groped her.
Manya told police that Kumar then left the apartment, asking her to inform him whenever she had 10–15 minutes of free time. She alleged that he also told her that he liked her and wanted to be around her.
Ashok Nagar police have registered a case under Sections 74 (assault or use of criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty) and 75 (sexual harassment) of the BNS.
A senior officer said the accused was questioned as part of the investigation, and a notice was served on him for further inquiry. Kumar, however, told police that the allegations were false and claimed that Manya had made them after he questioned her about defaulting on rent payments.

briefs.headline: Botticelli’s Madonna and Child comes to Bengaluru
briefs.deck: The Renaissance painting is part of One Mother, Many Mother Tongues, a new exhibition, co-curated by Naman Ahuja and Andrea Anastasio, which explores how the visual motif of mother and child migrates across borders, changing identity according to region, religion, language, and culture
briefs.bodyText:
In the centre of a darkened gallery at the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA), Bengaluru, Sandro Botticelli’s Madonna and Child gleams within its gilded frame. The Virgin Mother, whose alabaster skin, high forehead, hooded eyes, elongated nose and jaw, and small but pronounced Cupid’s bow bear a striking resemblence to the women in the Italian Renaissance painter’s classic masterpieces, Primavera and The Birth of Venus, is dressed in colours which hint at Christian duality: her scarlet robe signifies her humanness and eventual sacrifice, while her blue mantle represents the cosmos, a nod to the divinity she has carried within her.
In her arms, she cradles a naked, chubby male child who looks away from her into the distance, her expression deeply melancholic. “She knows what is to come,” says art historian and academician Naman Ahuja, pointing out other details in the painting that foreshadow Christ’s crucifixion, death, and resurrection, such as the architectural framing of the background, which resembles a cross, and the stone gargoyles behind Mary, a visual warning.
While Botticelli’s Madonna and Child, a 93 × 73 cm tempera and oil tempera on wood panel, is indeed a masterpiece, it is not the only one on display at this new exhibition, One Mother, Many Mother Tongues, co-curated by Naman and the director of the Italian Cultural Centre in India, Andrea Anastasio. The result of a collaboration between the Consulate General of Italy in Bengaluru, the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA) and the Ministry of Culture, it has been supported by the Prestige Group, with Rezwan Razack’s Museum of Indian Paper Money as cultural partner.
Some of the other artworks, which are part of the exhibition, include a tiny, 4500-year-old terracotta sculpture from Harappa, a delicate ivory carving of a mother balancing a girl (the only image, which depicts a female child) on her head from Bengal, statuesque stone effigies of ancient Indian goddesses like Chamunda, Skanda Mata, Matrika, Hariti and Jyeṣṭhā and a collection of Etruscan representations of Mater Matuta, an indigenous goddess of fertility, childbirth, and ripening grain, later co-opted and syncretised by the Romans.
These artefacts, spanning geography, cultures, media, and millennia, collectively dissect how a persistent visual motif—mother and child—migrates across borders, changing identity according to region, religion, language, and culture, as the exhibition release states. “Through these images, it explores how birth represents not only the creation of physical life, but also the emergence of ideas, beliefs, and cultural identities.”
It also notes that the exhibition examines how images shape and reinforce ideas within societies, inviting reflection on other questions that remain relevant today: Is motherhood the primary framework through which the feminine is granted agency? How have societies defined parenthood and gender roles through visual culture? Do ancient representations of the feminine always need to be understood through the lens of the Mother Goddess?
Genesis and more
The idea for the exhibition emerged out of a casual conversation between the two curators. Andrea, says Naman, had read a paper he had published some years ago, also titled One Mother, Many Mother Tongues, and “wanted me to expand it into an exhibition, because he had the opportunity to bring a Botticelli to India, and knew that for it to speak to people here, it might actually need to be complemented with other images that have the history and story of the mother in India.”
After all, the Botticelli is, as Naman points out, the inheritor of a very long past, “with many ideas of cultural continuity carrying on into the mother and child in Christianity.” Even though the church would not have wanted to give Mary such importance, “every town and village in Europe had their patron goddesses, and when Christianity rose, those goddesses were subsumed by Mary,” he says.
And, yes, this past also includes a long, shared history between India and Europe. While intercontinental trade has existed for millennia, by around 200 CE, as large, powerful empires like the Romans, Kushans and Satavahanas began to flourish, “it gets really intensified.” Maritime trade has exploded because they’ve just discovered how to use the monsoon to their advantage, and ships between India and Egypt are plying constantly, while the Silk Road is really active, he says. “Roman goods were coming to India, and vice versa.”
It was not just precious metal, spices, textiles, ivory, gemstones, and ceramics travelling across continents, but also tremendous cultural and religious exchange that enriched these ancient worlds without flattening them. “Through 26 masterpieces, it tells of this complex, shared history between the Mediterranean and India, and this dialogue carries on across the gallery,” says Naman, who believes that while the concept of the mother is a universal one, once it is teased open, “you will see the extraordinary diversity that is lying encapsulated within that concept of one mother, where many mother tongues are speaking their own languages through that same image. There is great unity, but if you look deeper into it, you will also see the extraordinary pluralism that we are able to maintain.”
Politically speaking, this is an important discussion in our times, where people often worry that globalisation results in cultural homogenisation, believes Naman. “An exhibition like this gives us the confidence to know that throughout history, every culture has managed to keep its own identity, even though there are extraordinary forces of homogenisation and globalisation around us,” he says. “I wish more people would recognise the fact that while there is a constant flow of ideas and culture, and these things will continue to flow, there has always been power in society to be able to hold onto your culture, regardless of whatever forces there may be around you, to try and alter that.”
One Mother, Many Mother Tongues will be on view from August 20 to September 20 at the National Gallery of Modern Art, Bengaluru.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru: Poor rains and sowing, festive demand drive up prices of vegetables
briefs.bodyText:
With the festival season set to start with Varamahalakshmi on Friday (August 21) followed by Ganesh Chathurti, accompanied by deficit rain and a decrease in sowing percentage, vegetable prices in different markets of the city have increased.
Gangadhariah, a vegetable trader at Kalasipalya vegetable market in Bengaluru, said, “Traders buy vegetables from here in large quantities and sell them in bigger markets like Shivajinagar, Yeshwantpur, Gandhi Bazaar, K.R. Market, Madiwala and others. Last week, the price of onion per kg in the wholesale market ranged somewhere between ₹17 and ₹28 depending on the quality and size. Now, it has increased to ₹32-35 depending on the quality. In retail, it will be ₹50 to 55 per kg, and first-grade ones have gone up to ₹60 per kg.”
He added, “Since onion is used as an ingredient in most of the dishes prepared at home, the demand is high. In addition, less rainfall and less stock in the market has lead to price surge during festival season. We usually depend on Maharashtra for onions and this year, we will to have purchase more than the expected load that arrives every year.”
Vishwanath Patil, president of Jai Kisan Wholesale Vegetable Market in Belagavi, noted that if it continues to rain, it is good for farmers but bad for the traders. “We purchase onions and tomatoes from Maharashtra and Chitradurga respectively. However, if it rains, half of the stock will get wet and rot away in crates even before it reaches us. In such a case too, the prices of these vegetables will increase, impacting the consumers,” said Mr. Patil.
Meanwhile, Valliammal, a vegetable vendor in Vasanth Nagar, also highlighted that the retail prices of vegetables have started increasing from the past two days owing to the upcoming festival.
She said, “People think that vegetable vendors earn well by charging more for vegetables. But on festivals, we do not earn a profit of even ₹100 because the prices at wholesale markets or APMC mandis are also high. On normal days, after deducting expenses, we easily gain profits of ₹200-400 per day.”
Quoting the prices of vegetables, she said, “At present, the price of onion is ₹50-55 per kg depending on the size and quality. Last week, it was ₹40 per kg. Tomatoes, which were ₹30-35 are priced at ₹40-45 per kg, while bajji chilli is ₹70 per kg and will increase up to ₹80-90 per kg on Thursday and Friday. Green chilli, which was ₹60 per kg, has increased up to ₹80 per kg. Beans is ₹90 per kg and carrot has increased from ₹70-88 per kg. This year, because of deficient rain, high demand and low stock in wholesale markets, the prices have surged.”

briefs.headline: Sharing circles launched in Bengaluru as part of Manotsava 2026
briefs.deck: Some of the issues which are being discussed in these circles include adoption, managing family expectations, finding support systems, reflecting on midlife, negotiating difficult family dynamics, and supporting caregiving
briefs.bodyText:
Rema, an adoptive parent to a two-and-a-half-year-old girl, is deeply aware of the impact of childhood experiences and parenting style on the development of children. “I keep reading about things and am in touch with other adoptive parents,” she says.
This is perhaps why Rema found a recent sharing circle held in Bengaluru, titled The Adoption Conversation: When do you begin? How do you continue?, interesting. “I wanted to hear how other people are tackling the same situation.”
Having a platform like this, where everyone is on the same page, made it easier for her to walk in and share her thoughts, without judgement, explains Rema, who prefers to go by only her first name. “Every parent’s story is different, so having a space to share was beautiful.”
These sharing circles are part of a series organised as precursors to Manotsava 2026, an annual mental health festival co-hosted by Rohini Nilekani Philanthropies (RNP), NIMHANS and the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS).
In addition to adoption, this series will also include conversations about family expectations, finding support systems, reflecting on midlife, negotiating difficult family dynamics, and supporting caregiving, among others, in a safe, accepting space.
“I’ve always felt it to be powerful when you are able to speak your mind to someone and say what’s on your mind without being judged or having someone jump in and try to help you,” says Lakshmi Pattabi Raman, one of the sharing circle’s facilitators and an adoptive parent herself. This is especially true, Lakshmi believes, when the other people in the room already get it.
“It is cathartic to speak with other people who share the same experiences, not with the intent of solving things, but because hearing it out sometimes lightens it. And there is also the sense of finding community, knowing that you are not alone and that there are people holding similar questions that puzzle, trouble, or stress them out,” Lakshmi says.
The idea for these circles emerged at the previous edition of Manotsava, according to Natasha Joshi, Chief of Strategy at RNP and the festival’s programme curator. “The idea was to essentially marry neuroscience and clinical expertise with lived experience and put together a credible format for discourse on mental health,” Natasha says of the festival, which is co-curated every year through an open call for proposals. However, some of the proposals they received covered pertinent topics, but did not necessarily have a clinical angle or neuroscience lens, points out Natasha.
So they decided to ask the people who suggested these topics whether, instead of speaking about them on stage in a talk format, they could hold space and do it as a much more intimate sharing circle, led by lived experience, Natasha says.
“It was a risk, in the sense that we didn’t know whether there would be a demand for it and how it would actually play out in the festival. But we discovered it was superbly well-received,” says Natasha, recalling how they ended up having to turn hundreds of people away since every sharing circle was running at maximum capacity, with 50 to 80 participants.
“We had this whole experience of not just realising that the demand is greater than the supply, but that absorption capacity for this kind of thing is greater than what one imagines.”
This positive reaction to the sharing circles led the team to take it beyond the confines of the festival. “We got feedback from not just the participants, but also the facilitators, who had people reaching out to them even after, saying that they didn’t know such a space existed and that they wanted more of it,” says Yashasvi Murali, Portfolio Manager, Mental Health and Gender, RNP, who has played a crucial role in putting together these sharing circles.
Given that the facilitators, too, saw a lot of “value and potential, and given that they were willing to give their time to do more of something like this, we built on this,” Yashasvi says.
The Manotsava team began by reaching out to many of these facilitators, taking their feedback to understand what worked and what did not before getting into programming, explains Yashasvi.
“One of the constraints at the festival is that there is only so much time and so many circles we can have. That is when we started thinking of having it pre-festival, expanding the window right from August with three months to follow,” Yashasvi says.
They also worked with facilitators to better understand how to bring diversity into these circles, not just in terms of themes and languages, but also trying to address the concerns and interests of people across age groups which move beyond mental distress or illness to experiences that are common but difficult to talk about. “It is an entire spectrum, and we tried to cater to different kinds of conversations about things people may experience and want to have.”
The sharing circles, which kicked off on August 1 and will run until October 31 at various locations in the city, are led by both people with lived experience of the issue and trained mental health professionals.
“We have around 19 circles this time in Bengaluru, and about half of them are entirely lived-experience-led, while the other half is being facilitated by a therapist or professional in some trained capacity,” says Yashasvi, pointing out that who leads a circle depends on the topic being addressed at the circle.
Irrespective of who is facilitating the session, there will be a clinician in the room, on standby for support, in case someone needs help, Yashasvi further adds. “While we may be looking at broader questions and themes, for a lot of people, it is the first time they’ve opened up, and this really unlocks emotions they haven’t tapped into in the past. In some cases, having this support is good.”
The larger goal of the initiative, in Natasha’s opinion, is to break through the loneliness and isolation of modern society. “Not to jump the gun, but my hunch is that there is no other place that these participants have found where these conversations are happening like that,” she says. With the resounding response to the sharing circles initiative, the founders now hope to further expand the initiative, both within the city and beyond. “We would love for sharing circles to serve as an example of self-organising spaces that every community can build” says Natasha.
To know more, log into nationalmentalhealthfestival.com/sharing-circles

stories.headline: Irdai bars Niva Bupa's branch expansion for six months
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Niva Bupa Health Insurance has been barred from opening new places of business for six months after the insurance regulator found that the company had failed to comply with expense of management limits for 2024-25.
Irdai in an order issued Aug 19, also warned the insurer for the breach. Niva Bupa said it complied with the expense of management regulations for the year ended March 31, 2026, and the quarter ended June 30, and remains on track to comply with the rules for 2026-27.
The company said the order would have no quantifiable financial impact.
The action followed a regulatory examination of Niva Bupa's expenses for 2024-25. Irdai found that the insurer had not complied with Regulation 6, read with Regulations 10, 11 and 19, of the Irdai (Expenses of Management, including Commission of Insurers) Regulations, 2024.
The rules set limits on insurers' expenses, including operating costs and commissions. Regulation 6 prescribes the limits on expenses of management, while the other provisions cover the calculation, reporting and compliance requirements. Niva Bupa said it is evaluating the order and will take appropriate steps to safeguard the interests of stakeholders.

stories.headline: VW goes vocal for local with compact SUV
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Volkswagen is adopting a "vocal for local" strategy as the global automotive industry becomes more regional, Thomas Schafer, chief executive of Volkswagen Passenger Cars, said as he announced plans to launch a locally manufactured sub-four-metre compact SUV in India in 2027.
The made-for-India model is to be built on Volkswagen's MQB-A0-IN platform, which has been localised at Volkswagen's Pune operations.
It will be the brand's most accessible offering in the country. The company expects it to strengthen its presence in the compact SUV segment, one of the largest segments of India's passenger vehicle market.
Schafer said India had gained importance for both the Volkswagen brand and the wider group as global politics and changing trade dynamics reshaped the automobile industry. "The automotive industry has become more vocal for local or a more regional reorganised industry, which in the past it had not been," Schafer said. "Now we see cars made in China for China, we see a lot that happening here in India. We see a lot of dynamics in the US."
He said the shift created opportunities for Volkswagen to expand its presence in India into research, development and information technology. On the awaited local partnership, Schafer said "We are exploring all options with what we can do in India because it has such importance for us. 
And one of them is talking to a few local partners and we believe that that's a good way forward. But it's too early to now announce anything. It's not there yet. But it's also not years away".
Schafer said India's automotive ecosystem offered opportunities in the changed global environment. The company also saw scope to expand its links with Europe and other markets as trade agreements evolved. India already serves as an export base for Volkswagen, with vehicles shipped to more than 40 countries, including Mexico. Schafer said both sides had benefited from the relationship and that the company was willing to explore further opportunities. "India is a market of enormous scale and ambition, and this new compact SUV marks an important step in Volkswagen's journey here," Schafer said.
"We are bringing our global expertise in building cars that people love to drive and own into a segment of great importance to Indian customers. This model is being developed specifically for India, and it reinforces our long-term commitment to the Indian market as part of our global growth strategy."

stories.headline: Centre’s fiscal outlook faces geopolitical, revenue risks
stories.deck: Central government finances for 2026-27 may remain close to budgeted levels
stories.bodyText:
Geopolitical headwinds in the background of recently introduced tax changes would shape the Centre’s fiscal outlook for 2026-27. Despite pressure on tax revenues and subsidies, strong non-tax receipts and policy interventions may keep fiscal outcomes broadly on track.
As per the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) data, the Centre’s gross tax revenues (GTR) grew only by 3.7% in the first quarter of 2026-27. This was the result of subdued revenue performance of personal income tax (PIT) and Goods and Services Tax (GST), both of which were subjected to substantive modifications in 2025-26. In both cases, extensive rate rationalisation was undertaken. In the case of GST, there was a substantive rate reduction. The expectation was that while these reforms would entail an initial revenue sacrifice, subsequent expansion of the tax base would offset the revenue loss over time. PIT revenue growth in 2025-26 was only 0.037%, implying a buoyancy of zero. For the second half of 2025-26, GST revenue growth was 4.67%. The revenue reducing effect of these major tax interventions has continued in 2026-27. PIT shows a growth of 6.8% in the first quarter of 2026-27 while GST revenues showed a contraction of (-)11%.

stories.headline: Pulse Pharma gets DCGI nod for nano-carrier entrapped Vitamin D3 oral dispersion
stories.bodyText:
Pulse Pharmaceuticals has received approval for its nano-carrier entrapped Vitamin D3 oral dispersion from the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI).
The approval transforms advanced nano pharmaceutical research into a regulated, patient-ready product, the company said on Thursday.
Founder and Managing Director K. V. Rambabu said such an approval is probably first in the world. It is set to pave the way Pulse Pharmaceuticals to take the product to some of the neighbouring South Asian countries besides helping it in seeking regulatory approval in highly regulated markets, including the U.S.
The company, which he said has been working in nano pharmaceutical drug delivery since 2010 said uses nanotechnology to improve how well a drug works, its bioavailability, how easily it is tolerated and the overall patient experience. It has developed several proprietary platform technologies to effectively deliver medicines.
Beyond Vitamin D3, Pulse is applying these platforms to other essential nutrients such as Vitamin K2-7, Vitamin B12 and Iron as well as in widely used medications like Paracetamol, Diclofenac and Ibuprofen, he said.
The company said it holds five patents across India, the U.S., Russia, Mexico and Australia. An EU patent for its Aqueol technology is in the final stages of approval.
It has also has filed patents for 4 other proprietary platforms across 7 major countries and working on filing 3 more. “Our purpose has always been to identify important unmet needs in drug delivery and develop practical solutions that can make a meaningful difference to patients,” Mr.Rambabu said.

briefs.headline: Sensex CAS manipulated using large orders: Sebi
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The first Sebi order relating to the recently introduced Closing Auction Session (CAS) system showed how, using money power, large institutions could manipulate the system and turn loss-making trades into profits in their books.
In the order published late on Wednesday, Sebi's investigation into the matter showed that on Aug 13, the sensex's weekly options contracts were to expire, and Copthall Mauritius, an arm of the global financial sector major JP Morgan, had put in orders worth over Rs 191 crore in sensex constituents, which was 87% of the total value of all the trades in those stocks. In comparison, the next high-value trade was worth Rs 12.2 crore, or 5.5% of the total value of trade.
On that day, within a two-second period between 3.20.41pm and 3.20.43pm, Copthall had placed almost all the buy orders, most of which were substantially above the 'reference price', leading to a 362-point rise in sensex value.
That day, another spike in sensex was seen between 3.24.08 pm and 3.24.20 pm when sensex rose 133 points. This spike too came on the back of a large Copthall order, Sebi said.
JP Morgan declined to comment on the matter.
During the same CAS period, Mansi Share & Stock Broking placed aggressive sell orders between 3.21.03 pm and 3.24.59 pm, aggregating 12.65 lakh shares across eight sensex scrips, with a substantial portion placed materially below the reference price. Subsequently, the broker cancelled the entire block within a short period around 3.26.02 pm, the Sebi order said.
The third spike in sensex that day was of 405 points that came between 3.25.49 pm and 3.26.17 pm. "This movement involved another aggressive buy-order burst by Copthall and was further amplified when Mansi (Broking) cancelled its large outstanding sell orders, removing the sell-side pressure and causing the (indicative price) to rise sharply in presence of outstanding aggressive buy orders of Copthall."
The Sebi order also said that Mansi Broking also followed a similar strategy to turn options contracts, which otherwise would turn worthless on the expiry day, profitable through large order placement and then cancellation of those orders.
Sebi noted that for Copthall, a movement in the sensex from 77,820 points to 78,080 points "resulted in additional payoff on certain call positions and avoidance of payment on certain put positions." In the case of Mansi (Broking), Sebi found that it exited "certain sensex put positions while its aggressive sell orders were outstanding. It is observed that these positions would otherwise have expired worthless."
Sebi on Wednesday night banned both the entities from the market and ordered them to disgorge illegal gains of nearly Rs 3 crore from Copthall and Rs 76 lakh from Mansi Broking.

briefs.headline: Government to amend investment treaty to woo global players
briefs.deck: To Allow International Arbitration In A Year Instead Of 5 Yrs
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Seeking to address a long-pending grouse of overseas investors, govt is all set to amend the model bilateral investment treaty (BIT) to allow for international arbitration one year after exhaustion of local remedies, instead of the current five-year clause that was brought in, amid a spate of challenges by global investors.
A cabinet note has been moved by the finance ministry to amend the model BIT put in place a decade ago and it has also proposed to expand the definition of investment from enterprise-based to asset-based, which will include shares and equity instruments that are maintained for five years or more, persons familiar with the discussions told TOI.
Govt plans BIT overhaul, may open door to international arbitration after 1 year
The Centre is looking to provide certain carveouts, which can include aspects, such as subsidies, local govt measures and compulsory licensing used to waive patent rights in cases of public health emergency and other situations. Investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) can be used as the starting point for BIT negotiations, people in the know said.
BITs are international agreements between two countries, establishing terms and conditions for private investment. It provides for national treatment, which in India's case is post-investment and a dispute resolution mechanism. The first model BIT was put in place in 1993 as govt courted investors from across the globe and eased its FDI rules.
In 2015, after facing a record number of ISDS claims and losing a case involving an Australian company White Industries, govt had opted for a revamp of the model treaty to better protect its interests. It resulted in unilateral termination of most of the BITs, which is not acceptable to a majority of the country. In fact, some of the BITs planned with free trade agreements could not be finalised as the countries had concerns.
According to Unctad database, since 2018 only six countries have agreed to BITs with India, including Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, Brazil, UAE, Uzbekistan and Israel.
India's recent trade and investment agreements with EFTA nations, led by Switzerland, as well as those with Oman, the UK, and the India-Brazil BIT, provide only for state-to-state obligations and exclude investor-state arbitration. There have, however, been few exceptions. The India-UAE BIT provides for three years of "exhausting local remedies", while the one signed with Israel has a four-year period.
For several months, there was growing consensus within govt on the need to rewrite the model BIT, but it was being resisted by the finance ministry. Two weeks ago, economic affairs secretary Anuradha Thakur confirmed that govt will soon seek cabinet nod for changes to the model BIT. She had also said that govt will seek to ensure adequate protection for Indian investors too.

briefs.headline: 61.5% of women taking up G RAM G work shows positive indicator of rural livelihoods
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Over 11.4 crore person-days have been generated since the rollout of Viksit Bharat-Guarantee for Rozgar and Aajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act (VB G RAM G Act), which replaced 
MGNREGA
, according to the govt portal on the new scheme. Women account for 61.5% of the total person-days so far.
Even under the now-repealed MGNREGA, women's participation over the years was over 50%, with data available from 2013-14 indicating a rise, which saw 2023-24 witnessing the highest 58.9%. In 2025-26, the women person-days was at 57.25% .
While this is seen as a positive indicator of livelihood options for rural women, civil society organisations have over the years said that women comprise a growing majority as men often seek out open-market or male-specific agricultural wages that exceed the scheme's statutory payouts.
Amid continuing demands from states for raising the wages, revised wage rates were notified by govt, with a new interim base wage rate of Rs 300 per day when VB G RAM G scheme was rolled out from July 1. The national average notified wage was cited to have increased from Rs 298.8 per day under MGNREGA to Rs 327.4 under VB G RAM G, representing an average increase of Rs 28.6 per day. Prior to the notification, wage rates in several states were below Rs 300, with the lowest notified wage being Rs 241 per day.
However, the parliamentary standing committee on rural development and panchayati raj, in its report submitted last week in Parliament, reiterated its concern over the wages and recommended that the department of rural development carry out a comprehensive review of the wage-determination methodology, including the appropriateness of the 2011 base year and the adequacy of Consumer Price Index for Agricultural Labourers (CPI-AL). The panel recommended that the ministry consider instituting a minimum wage floor of Rs 400 per day with regional differentiation and ensure systematic and meaningful indexation to a robust inflation indicator that reflects actual rural living costs.
"Pending structural revision, necessary fiscal space should be sought for a significant upward adjustment in the current cycle," the panel chaired by Congress MP Saptagiri Sankar Ulaka said. The panel has sought an action taken report on the fresh recommendations from the department of rural development within three months.

briefs.headline: For 1st time in a decade, India to import 10 lakh tonnes of sugar
briefs.deck: Faces Possible 20% Decline In Opening Stock Of Sweetener
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Govt Thursday allowed the import of 10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar, the first such move in a decade, as it stared at a possible decline of at least 20% in the opening stock of the sweetener.
The move came soon after the food ministry ordered that no bulk consumer such as confectioners, soft drink manufacturers, food processing industries, sweetmeat sellers and other institutional buyers using more than 10 tonnes of sugar a month can hold inventories for more than 15 days. This means if an entity uses 12 tonnes a month, at any given point, it can hold a stock of six tonnes. The order will be applicable between Sept and Nov.
The low opening stock - projected at 35-40 lakh tonnes, against 50 lakh tonnes at the start of Oct 2025 - was on account of a sharp fall in production to 296 lakh tonnes, the lowest since the 2019-20 sugar season that runs from Oct to Sept. During the next crop year, the industry has estimated production at 324 lakh tonnes.
The sugar industry has maintained that there is no shortage in the country as stocks with mills are adequate to meet the domestic demand till Nov-Dec, when fresh sweetener reaches the market.
10 lakh tonnes of raw sugar to be imported as govt moves to curb price rise
Officials said India's annual sugar consumption is around 280 lakh tonnes. According to the third advance estimate of sugar production for the 2025-26 season in Feb, the industry projected net production at 290 lakh tonnes, excluding 31 lakh tonnes diverted for ethanol. The final sugar production figure for the current season is likely to be released next month.
Govt's twin moves come amid rising retail prices. The average sugar retail price was Rs 52.3 a kg Tuesday, 13% higher than a year ago, according to data available with the consumer affairs department. In July, retail prices rose over 9%. To check hoarding and speculative trading, govt imposed stock holding limits on sugar dealers from Aug to Nov and has made it mandatory for dealers to declare their stocks and update them weekly.
Indian Sugar & Bio-Energy Manufacturers Association said govt's move to import sugar sends a clear signal to the market that speculative and unwarranted price increases will not be allowed to persist. It said the import permission was a precautionary measure that added further comfort during the peak festival months, and not a response to any supply gap.

briefs.headline: NSE shares may trade on its platform under 'permitted-to-trade' route
briefs.deck: Under the permitted-to-trade framework, an exchange can allow trading in shares that are listed on another recognised stock exchange
briefs.bodyText:
The National Stock Exchange (NSE) may allow its shares to trade on its platform after being listed on a rival bourse, without requiring a separate approval from Sebi, as the proposed arrangement would fall under the exchange's existing 'permitted-to-trade' framework, an industry source said on Thursday (August 20, 2026).
The distinction is important as permitted-to-trade is not the same as listing. While a listed company has disclosure and compliance obligations towards the primary exchange where it is listed, the 'permitted-to-trade' framework only helps investors to buy and sell the security on another bourse.
Under the permitted-to-trade framework, an exchange can allow trading in shares that are listed on another recognised stock exchange. The company does not become listed on the exchange where its shares are permitted to trade.
"NSE may not be required to take Sebi approval for allowing its own shares to trade on the platform as far as it lists its shares on another exchange," the source familiar with the development said.
NSE already has more than 200 companies whose shares trade on its platform but are not listed on its platform, suggesting that trading on an exchange does not necessarily mean that the security is listed there.
The same mechanism is being used by other exchanges. MSEI and NCDEX together have around 4,000 companies whose securities are permitted to trade on their platforms even though they are not listed on those exchanges.
Such permitted-to-trade arrangements do not involve a separate approval from Sebi for each security, as the process concerns trading of securities and does not amount to a fresh listing.
The move could become significant for NSE as it prepares for its own public-market debut. If NSE lists its shares on another exchange, the shares could potentially subsequently be permitted to trade on NSE under the existing framework.
For investors, the practical outcome is that NSE shares could become available for trading on its own platform even though it would not be listed there.

briefs.headline: Investors dump India bonds after hawkish RBI minutes
briefs.deck: The yield on ⁠the benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond climbed 5 basis points to 6.8709%, its highest since June 15
briefs.bodyText:
A hawkish tone in the Reserve Bank of India's policy minutes jolted domestic bonds on Thursday (August 20, 2026), compounding pressure from rising oil prices and knocking the liquid 10-year benchmark to a two-month low.
The yield on the benchmark 6.94% 2036 bond climbed 5 basis points to 6.8709%, its highest since June 15. Bond yields move inversely to prices.
RBI minutes released on Wednesday showed policymakers were more prepared to raise rates if inflation risks materialise, with concerns mounting over higher food, fuel and input costs feeding into broader price pressures.
Governor Sanjay Malhotra said that evidence of such spillovers could warrant "policy tightening." The comments accelerated the bond selloff by reviving expectations of higher borrowing costs.
The MPC minutes showed a path being built to eventual hikes, Tanay Dalal, economist at Axis Bank, said.
"We continue to see hikes to a 6% neutral, with room for an October move opening. However, a December hike is far more likely," Mr. Dalal added.
